Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Vignette:
Arjun had been walking back to his painting studio after a late site job when the man approached from behind. He remembered the sudden pressure of a forearm against his chest, the sharp intake of breath, the wallet and phone disappearing into a jacket pocket before Arjun could speak. The attacker did not shout, did not swing, but moved with a quiet certainty that left Arjun standing alone on the cracked pavement. What frightened him most was the stillness that followed, the way the street lights hummed overhead while he stood frozen, certain the man would turn back. Over the following weeks, Arjun began waking with dream residue, the heavy warmth of the blanket unable to dispel the lingering sense of the encounter. He found himself pausing in familiar spaces, his gaze catching on the loading dock doors, the narrow walkway between buildings, the exact geometry of where he had been cornered. When a memory of the event would come to mind suddenly, it arrived as a physical flash rather than a story, complete with the faint smell of rain on asphalt and the sharp tension in his shoulders. His body settled into a permanent state of readiness. Alongside this, an irritability surfaced without warning; a misplaced brush, a delayed email, the sound of a heavy cart rolling past his studio door could draw an angry outburst, though he could not quite name what it was protecting him from. His scanning for danger occupied much of his attention, his eyes tracking hands, movements, the angles of doorways. This constant vigilance coexisted with a deep sense that he could not rely on the usual rhythms of daily life to hold steady. He began avoiding the downtown warehouse district, taking longer routes through familiar neighborhoods, which meant arriving early to job sites and waiting until the light softened before entering tight corridors. His wife, Priya, would call out from the kitchen, but he was accustomed to working alone now. What Arjun had come to believe was that people could not be trusted to notice what mattered, to move through the world without creating the same sudden pressure. He felt set apart from others, isolated even in crowded rooms, and his isolation rested quietly alongside his mistrust. When Arjun tried to deliberately remember what had happened, he found it difficult to access the full account. The memory felt incomplete, like a photograph developed only halfway, with the edges blurred and the central figures unclear. Yet, on the days he managed to pull the pieces together, guilt would rise on recall, sharp and unexpected, as if he had failed to protect himself or had somehow invited the encounter. His painting work continued, but the avoidance had concrete consequences; he declined a commission to paint a downtown gallery space, citing a need to monitor his studio’s climate control, and Priya noticed how he would step back when she reached for his hand, as though her touch might pull him into an unfamiliar current. He told himself it was simply a matter of space, of giving his muscles time to rest, but the truth was that he was conserving his alertness. Now, at twenty-nine, Arjun sits in a therapist’s office with the city visible through the high windows. He still wakes with the ghost of the dream residue, still tracks the footsteps in the hallway, still feels the familiar tightness coiled in his chest. He has come to seek help; the constant scanning and the sudden memories now crowd his work and his marriage, and the weight of staying ready sits heavily upon him. He fears the quiet return of the stillness that followed the mugging, the moment when he will once again stand alone while the world moves past. What he hopes for is simply a steadier rhythm, a way to move through the physical locations of his days without bracing for impact, and to trust that the memories he cannot easily reach are not lost, only waiting.
